newsitem.title: UK: Russia sentiment up, but investors await results.
newsitem.headline: Russia sentiment up, but investors await results.

text.p: Sentiment towards Russia has picked up following a recent government reshuffle and the return to health of President Boris Yeltsin, but analysts said concrete steps still needed to be taken to convince nervous foreign investors.
International Monetary Fund (IMF) head Michael Camdessus' comments on Wednesday that the time had come to resume lending to Russia were seen buoying sentiment.
Camdessus said in Moscow that the economy remained in crisis, but saw the possibility of single-digit inflation next year and six percent growth by 2000.

The IMF has repeatedly suspended monthly payments of a $10 billion loan -- one of the reasons that Camdessus is in Moscow for talks with government officials -- amid fears that Russian tax revenues, running well below budgeted levels, could undermine public finances.
"The most important immediate target is the revenue performance. The first half of March was not very good but last 10 days was better," said a London-based analyst who asked not to be identified.

He said fiscal performance, the resumption of IMF funding and the restructuring of Russia's powerful natural monopolies would be key factors to watch in the short term, adding that the general outlook had improved recently.
"The new energy level of President Yeltsin and the appointment of the new team is certainly cause for optimism but we have to wait and see on performance," he said.
"The issue is still a fiscal one, getting an appropriate revenue performance in order to sustain the budget and to maintain the momentum on the (reform) programme," he said.
Other analysts said the IMF was always likely to go ahead with the funding, but Camdessus' comments were encouraging.

"They are not going to pull the plug on Russia. It is too important a country to disappear. What they are trying to do is sort out tax collection and the fiscal problems," said Nigel Rendell, HSBC James Capel emerging market strategist.

"The IMF is very keen to keep the government on course so obviously now Yeltsin is back and (first deputy premier) Anatoly Chubais has started operating this can be seen as a seal of approval by the IMF," Vlad Sobell, senior economist at Daiwa said.
Rendell said Yeltsin's improved health had been the major factor driving an improvement in investor perceptions in recent months.

"Yeltsin is back in charge and he has got the reformers in, things are progressing hopefully on the reform process, inflation is continuing to come down and I am still looking for a bounce back in the economy in 1997," Rendell said.
Output has fallen since the beginning of economic reforms in 1992.
He said investors had moved away from top line stocks to the second tier, but he remained optimistic that the market would do well this year, with debt instruments also expected to perform.
Russian Bradys picked up earlier on Wednesday on hopes about the IMF lending programme.
